claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain in fusion plasma-facing structural alloys is governed by the density and spatial distribution of grain-boundary nanoprecipitates.
High-temperature toughness in fusion plasma-facing structural alloys is governed by the density and spatial distribution of grain-boundary nanoprecipitates.
The relevant nanoprecipitates form and remain stabilized at grain boundaries under high-temperature conditions.
Nanoprecipitates pin dislocations and hinder their motion.
Nanoprecipitates retard dynamic recovery mechanisms such as dislocation climb.
Retarding dislocation motion and dynamic recovery limits elevated-temperature plastic deformation.
Nanoprecipitate-mediated dislocation pinning enhances toughness by delaying crack initiation and propagation.
A nanoprecipitate-promoting thermal treatment can produce a higher density and more uniform distribution of nanoprecipitates at grain boundaries.
Samples with an engineered higher nanoprecipitate density will exhibit less high-temperature plastic strain than untreated controls.
Samples with an engineered higher nanoprecipitate density will exhibit a lower high-temperature creep rate than untreated controls.
Samples with an engineered higher nanoprecipitate density will exhibit greater high-temperature fracture toughness than untreated controls.
The proposed relationship should hold in the plasma-facing-component temperature regime while the nanoprecipitates remain stable.
The upper temperature boundary for precipitate stability is approximately 1000°C.
The proposed relationship is expected to apply to alloys with compositions similar to that of the unspecified baseline alloy.

Failure to observe lower plastic strain and greater toughness in the engineered samples, or failure to observe a relationship between nanoprecipitate density and dislocation mobility, would falsify the hypothesis.
